newsitem.title: south korea: U.S., Seoul seen moving to defuse Korean tensions.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Seoul seen moving to defuse Korean tensions.

text.p: A U.S.-South Korean agreement to reaffirm an invitation to North Korea to join talks has set the stage for a flurry of diplomatic activity aimed at defusing tensions on the Korean peninsula, analysts said on Monday.

President Bill Clinton and South Korean leader Kim Young-sam on Sunday called on Pyongyang to take unspecified "acceptable steps" to end a crisis caused by the North's submarine incursion in September.

But Clinton and Kim, meeting in the Philippines on the fringes of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, reaffirmed their support for proposed four-nation peace talks, which would also involve China.

The United States and South Korea jointly proposed the four-nation talks in April, inviting North Korea and China to join a dialogue aimed at replacing the truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War with a lasting peace. North Korea has not agreed to take part.

A South Korean presidential spokesman, speaking at Subic Bay in the Philippines where the APEC summit was held, said Kim told Clinton that once the North agreed to the talks the main task would be to "obtain an apology over the submarine incident and an assurance that such a provocation would not be repeated".
He told Reuters that meant talks could be held before an apology was made but as soon as talks are held the first task would be to obtain an apology.
Asked if that was a change in South Korean policy, he said: "It's not a departure but we are being a little more flexible to obtain the same objective."
Seoul had previously said it would freeze all contacts and assistance to the North, including financing a U.S.-North Korean nuclear deal, until it apologises for the submarine incident.

"This is a major softening of the stand by Seoul and the start of peace moves," said Lee Seo-hang, chief analyst on North Korea at Seoul's state-financed Institute of Foreign Affairs and National Security.

A North Korean submarine landed 26 agents on a South Korean beach after their submarine ran aground off the eastern city of Kangnung in September. South Korean soldiers killed 24 of the agents, one was captured alive and another is still at large.

In another conciliatory move, Kim said Seoul was committed to the 1994 U.S.-North Korean nuclear deal which halted the North's suspected arms project in return for nuclear power plants and interim energy.

"Now the ball has been tossed over to the North Korean side. South Korea cannot behave as if nothing happened after the September submarine incursion and some gestures should be made by Pyongyang before any cooperation resumes," Lee said.

Park Hun-ok, senior research fellow at the private Institute of North Korea Studies in Seoul, noted that steps to lower tension had already begun with the visit of U.S. Congressman Bill Richardson to North Korea.

Richardon, a Democrat from New Mexico, is to act as an unofficial U.S. envoy in talks with Pyongyang officials to bring back American detainee Carl Hunziker, a U.S. official in Tokyo said. He was due to arrive in Pyongyang on Monday.
Hunziker, 26, was arrested in August after crossing the Yalu River from China into the North and accused of being a U.S. spy. His family has denied the charge, saying he is a missionary.

"Clinton is confirming his policy of engagement with North Korea which contrasts with the strangle policy pursued by his predecessor George Bush," Park said. "Richardson, without doubt, will discuss other issues with North Korea during this trip."
Seoul, in another signal it does not want further tensions on the peninsula, said it would send home on Tuesday a North Korean sailor rescued while drifting off a southern island.
